### The Diary: Section 30

_Mid-book rhythm_

> January 1661⁠–⁠62 January 1st. Waking this morning out of my sleep on a sudden, I did with my elbow hit my wife a great blow over her face and nose, which waked her with pain, at which I was sorry, and to sleep again. Up and went forth with Sir W. Penn by coach towards Westminster, and in my way seeing that the Spanish Curate1281 was acted today, I ’light and let him go alone, and I home again and sent to young Mr. Penn and his sister to go anon with my wife and I to the Theatre. That done, Mr. W. Penn came to me and he and I walked out, and to the Stacioner’s, and looked over some pictures and maps for my house, and so home again to dinner, and by and by came the two young Pens, and after we had eat a barrel of oysters we went by coach to the play, and there saw it well acted, and a good play it is, only Diego the Sexton did overdo his part too much.

### The Diary: Section 4

_Dialogue and character voice_

> Particulars of the Life of Samuel Pepys The family of Pepys is one of considerable antiquity in the east of England, and the Hon. Walter Courtenay Pepys2 says that the first mention of the name that he has been able to find is in the Hundred Rolls (Edw. I, 1273), where Richard Pepis and John Pepes are registered as holding lands in the county of Cambridge. In the next century the name of William Pepis is found in deeds relating to lands in the parish of Cottenham, co. Cambridge, dated 1329 and 1340 respectively (Cole MSS., British Museum, vol. i, p. 56; vol. xlii, p. 44). According to the Court Roll of the manor of Pelhams, in the parish of Cottenham, Thomas Pepys was “bailiff of the Abbot of Crowland in 1434,” but in spite of these references, as well as others to persons of the same name at Braintree, Essex, Depedale, Norfolk, etc.
